About the growth model
The Student Growth Percentile (SGP) Methodology is an open
source norm- and criterion-referenced growth analysis method.
The norm-referenced component of the model is the student growth
percentile which indicates the growth a student makes.
Student growth percentiles can be cohort (peer) referenced or
baseline (non-peer) referenced.
The criterion-referenced component of the model is the student
growth percentile target which indicates the amount of growth
required by the student to reach/maintain desirable achievement
goals in a specified time frame. For example, catching-up to
proficiency within 3 years.
The norm- and criterion-referenced components together allow
stakeholders to understand what is, what should be, and what is
reasonable simultaneously.
The goal of the metric was to assist states to move beyond debates
over what “thermometer" is best to discussions of how best to use
the “thermometer".

Why Student Growth?

Where you are today is a result of where you started and how quickly
you’ve travelled since.
Distrance = Rate × Time.
In education, where a student starts if often out of the schools
control.
However, once in the school, the general belief is that we have some
control over how quickly a student "travels".
Those students who start behind have to travel more quickly to
catch-up given a fixed amount of time to reach the destination (e.g.,
12 years).
Those students who start ahead don’t have to travel as quickly to
reach the desired destination on time.

Describing Student Growth

Measuring student growth, even with a vertical scale, is not a simple
task.
Some believe a vertical scale simplifies the task of measuring
student growth.
Even with an interval (or ratio) scale, growth is not easy to interpret.
Consider, for example, height.
A child might grow 4 inches between ages 3 and 4.
4 inches is a well understood quantity.
The 4 inch increase becomes really meaningful only when understood
alongside the growth of other 3 to 4 year olds.
Student growth percentiles were developed to provide context for
describing and ultimately understanding student growth.

Student Growth Percentiles
Should we be surprised with a child’s current achievement given their prior
achievement?
Given a student’s prior scale scores and the associated conditional
density, their current scale score corresponds to a percentile of that
conditional distribution.
This percentile is the student’s growth percentile.
Growth percentiles are closely related to estimating the probability of
observing a student’s current achievement taking account of their
past achievement:

Pr(Current Achievement |Past Achievement ).
As such, growth percentiles describe the rarity of a student’s current
achievement conditional upon their prior achievement.

Student Growth Percentiles

Should we be surprised with a child’s current achievement given their
prior achievement?
Student growth percentiles answer this question.
Consider a low achieving student with 50th percentile growth and a
high achieving student with 50th percentile growth.
The low achieving student grew at a rate exceeding 50 percent of
similar students.
The high achieving student grew at a rate exceeding just 50 percent of
similar students.
The low achiever’s growth is probabilistically as rare as the high
achiever’s.
Equally rare does not mean equally good.
Judgments about the adequacy of student growth require external
criteria.

Two Flavors of Growth based Accountability

Our work in the last few years investigating growth/value-added models
has led us to believe that there are two general types of growth based
accountability

Norm-referenced growth based accountability.
Criterion-referenced growth based accountability.
These two approaches to growth impart different levels of stringency
Norm-referenced Is the group of students growing better/worse (on
average) than statistical expectation?
Criterion-referenced Is each student in the group growing at a sufficient
rate (i.e., targeted growth) to reach/maintain a desired
level of achievement (e.g. Pass or Pass +)?

Norm-referenced student growth/accountability

Using student growth percentiles, the median SGP for a group
describes whether students in the group, on “average”,
demonstrated growth above or below expectation.
This is essentially, what value-added models quantify.
Value-added models go an extra step an implicitly infer causality by
labeling the aggregate measure as a school or teacher effect.
Some value-added models include student level characteristics
(e.g., demographics) and thus set differential expectations.
Student growth percentiles do not include student level
characteristics in the model. Any adjustments needed for
accountability purposes can occur post-hoc.

Criterion-referenced student growth/accountability

Former Secretary of Education Margaret Spellings initiated the
Growth Model Pilot Program allowing states to include growth as a
means of satisfying AYP.
The “Bright Line Principle” of all students being proficient by 2014
remained.
15 states were accepted as part of the pilot. None saw a significant
improvement in their AYP numbers because of the
growth-to-proficiency goals.

Criterion-referenced student growth/accountability
The reality in all state education systems I have worked with is that
students who start behind tend to stay behind (Minimal or Basic) and
students who start ahead tend to stay ahead (Proficient or
Advanced).
Targeted growth (criterion-referenced growth) reflects this
unfortunate reality: Schools serving the lower achieving students will
likely have low percentages of students reaching their growth targets
and schools serving high achieving students will likely have high
percentages of students reaching their growth targets.
Alone, criterion-referenced growth (i.e, growth to proficient) provides
an impoverished view of student growth.
This is not to say that criterion-referenced growth is unimportant. It
must be balanced with a norm-referenced view of student progress.
The SGP methodology’s norm and criterion-referenced components
attempt to strike that balance allowing stakeholders to understand:
What is? , What should be? and What is Reasonable?
simultaneously.
